title: Detection of Email Accounts
summary: This strategy detects Email Accounts, the resource development technique in which an adversary creates or compromises mail accounts to support phishing, social engineering, and command and control. It matters because a mailbox is both a delivery channel and a believable identity: messages from a real looking account bypass user suspicion and often bypass authentication checks when the domain is properly configured. Detection relies on mail platform audit logs for mailbox creation, sign in logs for impossible travel and failed multi factor attempts, mail flow logs for high volume sending from new accounts, and inbox rule change events. It fails most often because the creation happens on external free providers beyond your visibility, and because marketing and automation systems create and use mailboxes constantly, so internal rules must be scoped by identity and domain.

beginner.definition: This detection watches for new or misused email accounts linked to your organisation. An email account is a mailbox that can send and receive messages. The detection looks for accounts created outside the normal process, or existing accounts used in strange ways.
beginner.whyItMatters: A believable mailbox makes a phishing message far more effective. Attackers use mail accounts to send fake invoices and password reset requests. They also use them to receive replies and to hold stolen data. Mailboxes created without oversight often go unnoticed for a long time. Watching creation and sign in activity closes that gap.
howItWorks: The mail platform writes an audit record when an administrator or user creates a mailbox.
Sign in logs record the address, the device, and the result of each login attempt.
The rule flags mailbox creation by accounts or methods outside the standard joiner process.
It adds sign ins from new locations and repeated multi factor failures on the same account.
Mail flow records show sudden bulk sending from an account with no sending history.
Analysts verify the account owner and disable anything that cannot be explained.
beginner.example: Think of a company letterhead. Anyone can type your logo at the top of a page. The paper looks official, so the reader trusts it. A mail account is that letterhead. It is cheap and quick to make one that looks real. The detection checks the print room log to see who ordered new letterhead and when.
takeaways: A mailbox gives an attacker both a delivery path and a trusted identity.
New mailbox creation tied to no joiner record is one of the clearest internal signals.
External free mail providers are largely invisible, so user reporting and inbound filtering matter too.

objectives: Explain how mail accounts support phishing and social engineering operations
Identify mailbox audit, sign in, mail flow, and inbox rule telemetry
Detect mailbox creation that has no matching joiner or change record
Recognise suspicious sign in patterns such as new geography or repeated multi factor failures
Design a response that disables the account and checks for sent messages
dataSources: Microsoft 365 unified audit log entries for new mailbox creation and mailbox permission changes
Mail platform sign in logs with source address, client application, and multi factor result
Exchange message tracking logs recording sender, recipient count, and message volume per hour
Inbox rule change events from mail audit logs showing forwarding or deletion rules
Human resources joiner records compared against new account creation events
logic: The pattern is mail account activity that does not match a business process: a mailbox created by an unusual administrator account or through a non standard method, a new account that sends a burst of similar messages within hours of creation, sign ins from a country the organisation does not operate in, or a forwarding rule added to an account that redirects mail externally. The fields to correlate are the mailbox identity, the creating account, the creation timestamp, the sign in source address, the send volume, and any rule change. Benign cases are legitimate new starters, shared team mailboxes, and marketing platforms that create sender accounts in bulk with a documented change ticket. The malicious case is creation without a joiner record, followed quickly by bulk sending or an external forwarding rule.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Mailbox Created Outside Joiner Process And Used For Bulk Sending
# logsource:
#   product: azure
#   service: exchange
# detection:
#   selection:
#     Operation: 'New-Mailbox'
#   filter:
#     InitiatingUser|contains: 'svc-hr-provisioning'
#   condition: selection and not filter
# level: medium
falsePositives: Automated onboarding systems that create mailboxes before the human resources record is synchronised
Marketing and support platforms that provision sender mailboxes in bulk for campaigns
Contractors and temporary staff whose accounts are created by a project administrator
Migration projects that recreate mailboxes in a new tenant or region
tuningNotes: Baseline mailbox creation by initiating account, creation method, and time of day, then filter the documented provisioning service accounts and allow those identities to create accounts freely. Correlate each creation against the joiner feed and alert only when no matching record exists within twenty four hours. Add send volume and forwarding rule conditions so that a new account is only high severity once it is actually used. Narrowing to the joiner comparison reduces noise but depends on feed quality, so monitor the comparison itself and treat missing human resources data as a coverage gap rather than as a clean result.
